# Taxonomy and decision space

**Problem → Decision → Alternatives → Trade-offs → Evaluation → Research.**
These fourteen domains are knowledge responsibilities, not fourteen mandatory pipeline stages. Domains 01–09 describe core ER decisions; 10–12 own research/evaluation; 13–14 own system-level constraints. Scoring and clustering are not interchangeable terms. Related-to edges do not establish same-as membership.

| Domain | Responsibility | Main question |
|---|---|---|
| [01](domains/01-problem-identity.md) | Problem Formulation & Identity Semantics | What does one entity mean, and what output constitutes a correct resolution? |
| [02](domains/02-architecture-orchestration.md) | Pipeline Architecture & Orchestration | How should components interact, route work and revise decisions? |
| [03](domains/03-data-integration.md) | Data Understanding & Integration | Which observations are semantically comparable and sufficiently reliable to use? |
| [04](domains/04-normalization-enrichment.md) | Normalization & Enrichment | Which transformations make values comparable without erasing identity evidence? |
| [05](domains/05-candidate-retrieval.md) | Candidate Generation & Retrieval | Which pairs merit scoring under a candidate budget, and which true matches could be missed? |
| [06](domains/06-comparison-evidence.md) | Comparison Features & Evidence Engineering | What similarities, contradictions and contextual observations should a scorer see? |
| [07](domains/07-matching-scoring.md) | Matching & Scoring | How should evidence be aggregated into a score whose interpretation is clear? |
| [08](domains/08-decision-resolution.md) | Decision Policies & Entity Resolution | When should a score trigger a link, abstention, assignment or entity-membership change? |
| [09](domains/09-master-maintenance.md) | Master Entity Construction & Maintenance | How should resolved entities be represented, updated and corrected without hiding evidence? |
| [10](domains/10-ground-truth.md) | Ground Truth & Labeling | What labeled evidence supports training, evaluation and diagnosis for the actual target population? |
| [11](domains/11-evaluation-diagnostics.md) | Evaluation & Diagnostics | Which measurements reveal local quality, final identity quality and the cost of errors? |
| [12](domains/12-experimentation.md) | Experimentation & Research Methods | Which controlled test would distinguish mechanisms and reduce decision uncertainty? |
| [13](domains/13-scalability-execution.md) | Scalability & Execution | How can a logically valid ER design fit resource and update constraints without concealing quality loss? |
| [14](domains/14-governance-monitoring.md) | Explainability, Governance & Monitoring | How can users understand, audit, correct and monitor identity decisions safely? |

## Boundaries that prevent duplicate knowledge
- Source profiling: **03**; quality-aware evidence: **06**; learned weighting: **07**.
- Single-record transformations: **04**; pair comparisons: **06**.
- Retrieval logic: **05**; physical execution/index maintenance: **13**.
- Score interpretation/calibration: **07**; score-dependent actions and membership: **08**; consumer entity construction: **09**.
- Label construction: **10**; measurements: **11**; experiment procedures: **12**.
- Lifecycle/topology: **02** with resource details in **13** and identity-state consequences in **09**.

## Cross-cutting dependencies
Normalization changes retrieval keys and evidence. Retrieval changes the score/calibration population. Scoring quality does not guarantee entity-quality improvement. Membership decisions affect master attributes and future graph features, which can feed errors back into matching. Privacy constraints can remove otherwise available evidence. Labeling, monitoring and experiments must evaluate these interactions rather than attributing all errors to a matcher.

See [independent architecture dimensions](architecture-dimensions.md), [conceptual contracts](module-contracts.md), [catalog](../CATALOG.md), and [reconciliation](../guides/design-reconciliation.md). Pilot method coverage is deliberately narrower than this taxonomy; the [expansion plan](../guides/expansion-plan.md) records the gap.

# Design comparison evidence before choosing a scorer

## Decision question and problem context

What information should a pairwise comparison expose so downstream scoring can distinguish identity support, uncertainty, and genuine incompatibility? Fellegi–Sunter comparison vectors explicitly allow agreement, disagreement, missing values, and partial address agreement rather than requiring one generic similarity number.[1] Evidence engineering defines those observations; it does not itself choose weights, probabilities, thresholds, or entity assignments.

The same similarity can have different implications across sources, identifier systems, and observation times. Retrieval further selects which pairs reach comparison. The [candidate strategy decision](candidate-strategy.md) therefore supplies context, while the [scoring decision](scoring-strategy.md) determines how evidence will be combined.

## Assumptions and prerequisites

**Atlas synthesis:** establish comparable field meanings, normalization lineage, validity checks, source provenance, observation times, and identity semantics. Preserve raw values alongside derived forms. Identifier comparison requires a namespace, issuing authority where relevant, and reuse or validity rules. An identifier can be lexically different without contradiction if namespaces differ; identical local numbers can be unrelated.

Determine what absent values mean: uncollected, unknown, redacted, failed parsing, or genuinely inapplicable. Missingness is neither observed agreement nor observed contradiction. It can nevertheless carry population-specific predictive information; that inference belongs in an explicitly tested scorer, not an undocumented comparison default.

## Alternatives and solution links

- [Explicit evidence states](../solutions/comparison-features/evidence-states.md): separate comparability, observed agreement, partial agreement, disagreement, and unavailable information. This is the expanded pilot baseline.
- **Taxonomy-only, unexpanded:** attribute-specific string, token, phonetic, and linguistic comparisons expose different variation; continuous values retain resolution but need documented meaning and missing-value handling.
- **Taxonomy-only, unexpanded:** frequency/rarity, source-quality, and temporal features qualify observations with context rather than replacing value comparison.
- **Taxonomy-only, unexpanded:** embeddings, relational context, multi-valued comparisons, and interaction features offer richer representations, with additional provenance and dependency questions. These are not linked to nonexistent Solution Cards.

A raw exact-agreement flag remains a useful controlled comparator, but collapsing every other outcome to one value loses the distinction between no information and contradictory information. Richer alternatives should address observed ambiguity rather than accumulate features indiscriminately.

## Choice criteria and trade-offs

**Atlas synthesis:** assess semantic validity, interpretability, transfer across source pairs and languages, availability, acquisition cost, and resilience to normalization errors. Compare what each feature reveals that existing features do not. For multiple aliases, specify whether comparison uses best agreement, overlap, or observed conflicting histories; maximum similarity can conceal disagreements and favors records with more opportunities to match.

A contradiction should require meaningful comparability and credible incompatible observations. A changed address is not inherently incompatible with enduring person identity. Shared household contact details may agree without being entity-unique. Reliability is contextual: source reputation alone does not establish accuracy for every field or time period.

Multiple representations of one name, parsed address components, and copied observations are potentially dependent evidence. The additive Fellegi–Sunter simplification assumes comparison groups are independent conditional on match status; the general joint formulation does not require that factorization.[1] The landscape discusses limitations of practical independence assumptions.[5] Preserve dependency groups instead of treating every transformation as independent corroboration.

## Baseline and related evaluations

**Atlas synthesis:** begin with a small attribute-specific evidence vector: explicit states, observed similarities where applicable, validity, and source/time context that is already available. Keep derived weighting separate. Compare this baseline against a collapsed-state representation and then add one contextual feature family at a time.

Use [pairwise quality and calibration evaluation](../evaluation/pairwise-calibration.md) with fixed candidate pairs, controlled scorer capacity, and source/entity-disjoint assessment where appropriate. Diagnose errors by evidence pattern and missingness segment, not only aggregate discrimination. Repeat after retrieval changes: agreement required by admission is not fresh independent support, and candidate-conditional distributions may differ from unrestricted-pair estimates. No evidence representation alone guarantees calibrated scores.

## Open questions and evidence limits

Can reviewers distinguish unavailable evidence from true conflict? Which apparently separate features descend from one observation? Does context improve transfer or merely encode source identity? The [frequency-aware hypothesis](../research/hypotheses/frequency-aware-evidence.md) and [contextual-reliability hypothesis](../research/hypotheses/contextual-reliability.md) propose tests, not validated improvements. The literature supports comparison-vector theory and dependency cautions, not this card's exact feature contract.[1][5] Recommendations are Atlas synthesis; no Atlas experiment has been run.

## Sources

[1] https://nhis.ipums.org/nhis/resources/Fellegi69.pdf — A Theory for Record Linkage
[5] https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.04443 — (Almost) All of Entity Resolution

# Explicit comparison evidence states

## Summary and problem addressed

Explicit states prevent a comparator from conflating absent information, noisy disagreement, and credible contradiction. Fellegi–Sunter comparison codes already distinguish missingness, agreement, disagreement, and partial agreement.[1] The state vocabulary and context contract below are **Atlas synthesis**, not a standardized taxonomy from that paper. They describe observations for scoring, not final match dispositions.

## Core mechanism

For each attribute, first establish semantic comparability: field meaning, representation, identifier namespace, and relevant time scope. Then record availability and validity on each side. Only compare values when the applicable prerequisites hold. Preserve the observed outcome, optional similarity, source/time provenance, and reasons for unavailable or unreliable comparison.

Use separate dimensions where states can coexist: lexical agreement can occur between invalid placeholders, and partial agreement can coexist with conflicting components. Do not force one label to erase quality context. An unobserved similarity should remain unavailable, rather than become a measured zero.

**Proposed vocabulary:**

- **Agreement:** comparable observed values agree under the declared representation; normalization-induced agreement remains distinguishable from raw equality.
- **Partial agreement:** observed values share specified components or graded similarity. Describe what agrees and what differs.
- **Observed disagreement:** comparable values differ; the comparison alone does not establish identity incompatibility.
- **Qualified contradiction:** credible observations violate an explicit identity constraint within a compatible namespace and time scope. Record the constraint and reliability rationale.
- **One-sided missing / both missing:** value comparison is unavailable, with side-specific missingness reasons retained.
- **Invalid or unreliable:** the observation or transformation fails a quality requirement; apparent equality need not be meaningful.
- **Incomparable:** meanings, namespaces, granularities, or temporal semantics do not permit the requested comparison.

Illustrative synthesis: two absent birth dates are both missing, not an agreement; a malformed date is invalid, not a different birth date. Different local identifiers from different issuers are not automatically contradictory. Historical addresses can disagree while remaining consistent with one person's movement.

## Theoretical explanation

A representation that maps missingness and valid disagreement to one value prevents every downstream scorer using only that representation from distinguishing those cases. Keeping states retains that information, though a larger feature space may require more estimation evidence. This is an information-preservation argument, not proof of better prediction.

Under likelihood-ratio scoring, a state contributes support according to how often it occurs among matches relative to nonmatches, not its label alone.[1] Thus observed agreement is not automatically strong support, and missingness is not inherently neutral or negative statistically. Treating missingness as identity evidence requires population-specific justification; its observational meaning remains absence of comparison. The additive simplification additionally requires conditional independence between evidence groups.[1]

## Variants, prerequisites, and applicability

**Atlas synthesis:** variants include categorical states, continuous similarities with availability masks, ordinal agreement levels, and component-level vectors for structured attributes. Multi-valued histories need explicit aggregation: best-pair agreement alone can hide contradictory observations. Preserve which values generated each outcome.

Prerequisites are attribute-specific semantics, trustworthy quality indicators, and accessible provenance. The approach is especially useful for sparse, heterogeneous, or conflicting records, but also makes clean-data defaults auditable. Several normalized forms of one value should share a dependency lineage, not count as independent facts.

## Advantages, trade-offs, and failure modes

States make explanations, missingness diagnostics, and controlled scorer comparisons possible. Costs include vocabulary design, sparse combinations, and maintaining consistent meaning across sources. A falsely declared contradiction can become an unjustified veto; a missingness feature can learn collection practices that fail under source shift. Copies and correlated transformations can still double-count evidence. The literature discusses practical dependency limitations; explicit states do not resolve them automatically.[5]

## Relationships and evaluation

This solution [addresses comparison evidence](../../decisions/comparison-evidence.md) and complements [additive soft matching](../matching-scoring/additive-soft-matching.md), [Fellegi–Sunter](../matching-scoring/fellegi-sunter.md), and [logistic regression](../matching-scoring/logistic-regression.md). Each supplies a different combination mechanism; no state is a prescribed weight.

**Atlas synthesis:** use [pairwise quality and calibration evaluation](../../evaluation/pairwise-calibration.md). Compare collapsed versus explicit states on the same candidates with controlled scorer capacity. Audit state assignment before measuring prediction; inspect missing, invalid, contradictory, source-pair, and temporal segments. Assess robustness after source shifts and retrieval changes, since candidate admission conditions observed evidence.

## Research opportunities and evidence limits

Test whether quality-qualified contradictions reduce harmful rejections, or source-specific missingness improves transfer rather than shortcuts. Ablate representation families and dependency groups. The precise contract remains synthesis informed by comparison-vector theory; no Atlas result establishes superiority.[1][5]

## Sources

[1] https://nhis.ipums.org/nhis/resources/Fellegi69.pdf — A Theory for Record Linkage
[5] https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.04443 — (Almost) All of Entity Resolution

# Choose a candidate generation strategy

## Decision question and context

Which record pairs should receive expensive comparison, under the project's coverage and resource constraints? Blocking restricts comparisons to records sharing blocks; similarity filtering instead excludes pairs using conditions tied to a specified similarity function and threshold. Their assumptions differ even when both reduce work.[2] Neither candidate membership nor exclusion should silently become a definitive identity judgment.

Define the admissible pair universe first: within-source deduplication, selected cross-source linkage, or both. Excluding prohibited source combinations is different from dropping plausible identities for efficiency. Candidate recall concerns true matching pairs admitted from this universe, not final cluster recovery.

## Assumptions and prerequisites

**Atlas synthesis:** establish identity granularity, identifier namespaces and validity periods, source-pair permissions, normalization contracts, and the acceptable consequences of missed matches. Profile field availability, key stability, common values, and block-size tails by source. Retain raw observations and retrieval provenance so exclusion causes remain inspectable. Labels collected only from current candidates cannot establish coverage outside that candidate set; use independently assembled identities or a defensible outside-set audit.

Do not assume missing fields are equal keys. Do not assume two copied sources provide independent corroboration. For identifier-based admission, lexical equality needs a compatible issuing namespace and temporal meaning, not merely matching characters.

## Available alternatives and solution links

- [Exact blocking](../solutions/candidate-generation/exact-blocking.md): economical, inspectable equality-based admission; sensitive to missing or corrupted keys. Composite keys demand agreement on every required component.
- [Multi-pass blocking](../solutions/candidate-generation/multi-pass-blocking.md): union complementary admission routes, preserving pass provenance and deduplicating pairs. Its value depends on newly exposed matches, not the number of generators.
- **Taxonomy-only, unexpanded:** sorted neighborhood exposes nearby ordering positions; approximate token/q-gram and inverted-index retrieval expose partial overlap; locality-sensitive hashing uses similarity-dependent collisions; vector retrieval searches an embedding space; learned and adaptive retrieval choose admission rules or budgets from data. These families are covered by the blocking landscape, but have no pilot Solution Cards here.[2]
- **Taxonomy-only, unexpanded:** similarity filtering may complement retrieval when its exclusion bound is valid for the intended comparison predicate; a heuristic rejection rule is not automatically such a guarantee.[2]

## Selection criteria and trade-offs

**Atlas synthesis:** compare mechanisms against observed corruption, rather than ranking families universally. Stable, populated keys favor exact admission. Multiple complementary attributes favor passes with different failure patterns. Text variation motivates testing approximate retrieval; representation and language coverage then become additional prerequisites. Learned retrieval needs representative evidence about both admitted and missed matches, with protection against source-specific shortcuts.

Measure unique pairs, retrieval work, downstream comparison cost, latency, memory, and coverage by source, script, sparsity, and key frequency. A broad pass may recover rare missed identities while flooding common-name blocks. A selective composite key controls cost but excludes matches whenever any required component changes. Duplicate candidates consume generation and deduplication work even if scored once.

**Mathematical reasoning:** adding a pass cannot reduce pair coverage if the admissible universe and truth set remain fixed and every old candidate survives. With ranking caps, block removal, sampling, or early stopping, this monotonicity no longer follows. Correlated passes may add substantial work without new matches. Distinguish losses at admission, budget enforcement, filtering, and scoring.

## Baseline and related evaluations

**Atlas synthesis:** begin with a small, documented exact-key strategy, plus a complementary pass only where profiling suggests a different recoverable failure. This is a diagnostic baseline, not a universally safe deployment choice. Compare alternatives with unchanged input representations and truth scope, then repeat under equal operational budgets.

Use [candidate recall evaluation](../evaluation/candidate-recall.md) to report pair completeness, reduction against the defined universe, unique candidate volume, segment gaps, and marginal coverage per pass. Inspect misses independently of scorer performance. The [comparison evidence decision](comparison-evidence.md) complements this choice because retrieval determines which agreements and contradictions the scorer can observe.

## Open questions and evidence limits

Which exclusions are unacceptable? Do large blocks contain recoverable matches or mostly ambiguity? Can sparse and multilingual records receive useful fallback routes? Does a new pass alter candidate composition enough to invalidate existing scoring estimates? The survey supports the method taxonomy and blocking/filtering distinction, not a recommended winner.[2] No Atlas benchmark has been run; baseline and experiment recommendations above are synthesis.

## Sources

[2] https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.06167 — A Survey of Blocking and Filtering Techniques for Entity Resolution

# How should candidate pairs be scored?

## Decision question

Which evidence-combination mechanism is defensible for the intended candidate population, and what meaning should its output carry: ordering, likelihood ratio, or estimated match probability? Choose a scorer independently of whether downstream resolution uses pairwise decisions, assignment, or clustering. Statistical linkage and entity-level reconstruction are related but distinct problems.[5]

## Problem context

Candidate pairs already reflect retrieval choices; their comparison vectors contain agreements, partial similarities, missingness, and contradictions. Scoring must combine these without silently treating duplicated representations as independent evidence. A shared surname can be weak evidence among surname-blocked candidates even when unusual among arbitrary record pairs. The [comparison decision](comparison-evidence.md) defines the evidence contract; the [candidate decision](candidate-strategy.md) defines which pairs the scorer will encounter.

## Relevant assumptions and prerequisites

Before selecting a family, document:

- Identity semantics, identifier namespaces, time validity, and permitted source cardinalities.
- Candidate-rule versions and inclusion provenance; changes alter the statistical target.
- Feature state definitions, missingness indicators, source reliability, and suspected dependencies.
- Available adjudicated labels, sampling design, unresolved cases, and entity-disjoint or temporal evaluation splits.
- Whether operations require only a rank order or defensible probabilities for explicit losses.

A numerical score is not evidence that these prerequisites hold. An unvalidated transformation into the interval zero to one does not establish calibration.

## Available solution families

- [Additive soft matching](../solutions/matching-scoring/additive-soft-matching.md): manually assign positive and negative contributions to explicit comparison features. Transparent, label-light, and useful as a controlled baseline; probability meaning requires additional justification.
- [Fellegi–Sunter](../solutions/matching-scoring/fellegi-sunter.md): estimate comparison distributions under matches and non-matches, then form likelihood ratios. The joint formulation does not require independent fields; the familiar sum of field weights requires conditional factorization.[1]
- [Logistic regression](../solutions/matching-scoring/logistic-regression.md): learn conditional log-odds from labeled comparison vectors. It does not require independent predictors, but its chosen feature basis constrains the conditional relationship.[7]
- **Unexpanded pilot families:** hard deterministic rules, generalized additive models, constrained models, boosted trees, neural matching, weak supervision, hybrids, and ensembles. These remain alternatives, not nonexistent card links. The broader literature contains diverse deterministic and statistical approaches.[5]

## Criteria for choosing

Prefer a reliable-identifier rule only when uniqueness, scope, and observation quality justify its semantics. Consider expert additive scoring when labels are scarce and explanations need explicit evidence accounting. Consider Fellegi–Sunter when comparison-state distributions can be estimated credibly, including candidate conditioning. Consider logistic regression when labels cover operational matches and difficult non-matches, and a manageable feature basis is plausible. Label abundance alone does not establish representativeness.

## Trade-off comparison

| Family | Weight interpretation | Principal burden | Important risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| Expert additive | Designed evidence points | Elicitation and sensitivity analysis | Subjective scale; compensating conflicts |
| Fellegi–Sunter | Joint or factorized log likelihood ratio | Estimating match/non-match distributions | Dependence and selection misspecification |
| Logistic | Conditional log-odds coefficients | Representative labels and model assessment | Sampling bias; unstable correlated coefficients |

These burdens follow the respective mechanisms.[1][7] Interpretability means knowing how contributions were obtained, not asserting that a coefficient is causal. Candidate selection can invalidate a transferred probability interpretation even if ranking remains useful; see the [selection and calibration deep dive](../deep-dives/selection-and-calibration.md).

## Good baseline candidates

Keep an expert additive specification and, where justified, a small reliable-identifier rule as interpretable reference points. Compare statistically learned weights on the same evidence states and candidates. Fellegi–Sunter and logistic regression offer different estimation routes, not successive maturity grades. Regularization, interactions, and additive nonlinear functions are optional responses to diagnosed limitations, not obligatory upgrades.[7]

Use [pairwise quality and calibration](../evaluation/pairwise-calibration.md) to compare ranking, probability reliability, and threshold sensitivity. Freeze features and candidate rules initially; reserve separate fitting, calibration, and final testing populations. Report source-pair and missingness slices, costs, and uncertainty. Then use [entity-resolution quality](../evaluation/entity-resolution-quality.md) under an unchanged resolution policy: better pairwise ordering need not establish better final entities.[5] Audit [candidate recall](../evaluation/candidate-recall.md) separately because scorers cannot rank omitted pairs.

Does disagreement come from weight estimation, missing evidence, or dependence? Compare manual versus learned contributions first, then ablate redundant representations or add one justified interaction. No method is declared universally optimal; no Atlas performance experiment has been run.

Fellegi–Sunter supplies stipulated-distribution decision theory, not automatic operational calibration.[1] ESL supplies general logistic foundations, not an ER superiority result.[7] The ER landscape supports scope distinctions, not a benchmark recommendation.[5]

# Thresholds, abstention, and review policies

## Short summary

Keep evidence estimation separate from the actions taken on its output. Link, non-link, and deferred review are distinct dispositions in classical linkage theory; the justified policy depends on distributions, error constraints, or losses rather than on an arbitrary confidence label.[1]

## Problem addressed

A useful ordering does not specify acceptable false-link risk, review workload, or permitted entity structure. A policy must translate scores into actions while respecting identity semantics, operational objectives, and downstream consequences. It should also distinguish a deferred unresolved pair from a confirmed non-match.

## Core mechanism

For a raw score, specify lower and upper operating thresholds: reject below the lower boundary, accept above the upper boundary, and defer between them. Fix boundary and tie handling explicitly. Select thresholds on representative validation labels under stated precision, recall, loss, or capacity requirements; do not use a probability formula on arbitrary score points.

For a **calibrated candidate-population probability** $p$, suppose correct actions have zero loss, false links cost $C_{FP}>0$, and missed links cost $C_{FN}>0$. **Expected-loss reasoning with these fixed pairwise losses:**

$$
R_{link}=(1-p)C_{FP},\qquad R_{nonlink}=pC_{FN}.
$$

Minimizing the two risks selects link when

$$
p>\frac{C_{FP}}{C_{FP}+C_{FN}},
$$

with an explicit tie convention. This is not a universal threshold: probability calibration, candidate population, action semantics, and the loss definition are conditions of the derivation. Context-dependent costs require conditioning on that context, not merely different thresholds without justification.

## Theoretical explanation

Introduce review risk rather than assuming review is perfect. **Illustrative risk model:**

$$
R_{review}=c_R+p\,e_{FN}C_{FN}+(1-p)e_{FP}C_{FP},
$$

where $c_R$ includes effort and delay, and $e_{FN},e_{FP}$ are review's conditional error rates. Select the minimum-risk feasible action. A middle abstention interval follows only if the risk functions cross appropriately; it is not guaranteed by three available actions. Capacity constraints can require prioritizing expected loss reduction per unit review effort. Uncertainty near a threshold is only one possible contributor to review value.

The landscape describes posterior-based expected-cost linkage decisions; the formulas here are explicit derivations under the stated assumptions.[5] Aggregate reliability is insufficient when costs or error rates differ across segments; validate probabilities at the information level used to act.

## Important variants

Single-threshold binary decisions, two-threshold deferred decisions, context-dependent thresholds, time-limited abstention, and workload-constrained review are policy variants. Formal assignment and constrained clustering are unexpanded pilot methods, not implied extensions of every threshold policy. A cost-sensitive threshold need not change the underlying scorer.

## Assumptions and prerequisites

Define the candidate population, loss units, permitted actions, and whether rejecting a candidate means no link now or a durable cannot-link. Estimate review accuracy and service capacity rather than treating annotation as infallible. Reserve independent test labels; thresholds chosen on the test set cannot support an honest prospective estimate. Document model and calibration versions, cutoff inclusivity, review expiry, and escalation ownership.

## Applicability conditions

Independent thresholds fit tasks with separable pairwise actions. If one-to-one linkage is required, several individually plausible pairs may compete for the same record. If the output is entity membership, pairwise decisions must be reconciled with the specified equivalence semantics and constraints.[5] These tasks require evaluating a resolution method, not merely tuning a cutoff.

## Advantages

Separating policy permits one scorer to support different loss profiles and review budgets. Explicit deferral preserves uncertainty and makes workload measurable. Stated risk assumptions allow policy changes to be audited instead of conflating them with improved scoring.

## Trade-offs and failure modes

Thresholds transfer poorly after candidate, source, or calibration shifts. A narrow review band can satisfy capacity while hiding dangerous accepted errors. Review delay can itself create loss. A hard veto is justified only by genuine semantic incompatibility backed by valid scope and observation guarantees; a noisy identifier conflict normally remains evidence, not a logical impossibility. Weak agreements must not arbitrarily override a legitimate constraint.

Connected components of accepted edges can amplify one false link into an overmerge; a rejected edge need not become a cannot-link.[5] Marginal pair probabilities are not automatically compatible partition probabilities.

## Relationships with other methods

Complements [additive scores](../matching-scoring/additive-soft-matching.md), [Fellegi–Sunter](../matching-scoring/fellegi-sunter.md), and [logistic regression](../matching-scoring/logistic-regression.md); their probability interpretations differ. A [precision cascade](../../architectures/precision-cascade.md) can route unresolved pairs to additional evidence or review rather than forcing immediate decisions.

## How to evaluate

Use [pairwise quality and calibration](../../evaluation/pairwise-calibration.md) for threshold sensitivity, accepted/rejected errors, and selective risk versus coverage. Measure review demand, delay, residual error, and cost. Use [entity-resolution quality](../../evaluation/entity-resolution-quality.md) for assignment violations, overmerges, and undermerges; pairwise gains alone do not establish safer entities.

## Research opportunities

Compare uncertainty-based review with expected-risk-reduction routing at a fixed budget. Treat review effectiveness and entity-level loss estimates as hypotheses requiring operational evidence, not automatic gains from abstention.

## References and evidence limitations

Classical disposition theory and later expected-cost formulations support the mechanism.[1][5] No project costs, reviewer accuracy, calibration result, or empirically optimal cutoff is supplied here.
